skip_reason: Post-move customer service call on two already-completed jobs, not a new-business sales conversation. Amanda Vandiver is an existing customer calling about debris left after a warehouse furniture pickup and a house-to-house move already performed and paid for ('I've had you guys do two jobs in the last two days for me'), asking whether Einstein will arrange the junk hauling her mover apparently offered. There is no lead, no quote form, no intake, no pricing pitch and no booking attempt — Rance is fielding a service complaint and trying to route her to the servicing branch. The 85-point sales scorecard does not apply and this call should not count toward the sales grading average.
top_strength: Rance held a clear, honest line on scope without waffling, which is the right instinct when a customer has been told something by a crew member that the company cannot deliver. He did not pretend the junk haul might happen to make the call easier — he named the boundary plainly ('we don't have facilities to dispose of materials like that. We generally you know, we're gonna move people') and, when she said the mover had implied it would be free, he corrected the expectation directly rather than letting it ride to the branch: 'that's not a free service for us either. So I don't know why the mover would have indicated that to you.' He also did not stonewall her — he agreed to the handoff she asked for and closed on an action: 'Yeah, I'll put you in contact with them... let me see what I can do for you.'
coaching_note: Lead with the acknowledgment, then the boundary — here it ran the other way, and the same 'no' delivered four times without any empathy in front of it is what turned a service question into a frustrated customer. She told him exactly what the problem was ('I have like a, like a really large pile of garbage that I have no idea what to do with') and what she felt about it ('We paid $600 for you guys to pickup furniture a job took like two hours and like, I just, I can't believe that'), and neither got a word of recognition before the next restatement of policy. One line — that it is frustrating to be left with the mess and he is sorry the crew set that expectation — costs nothing and does not concede the service. The second fix is to give her something instead of nothing: a junk-hauling referral, or Ecobox for the cardboard specifically, turns a flat no into a useful call. As it stands the most concrete thing she leaves with is a promise to be connected to someone else.
phone_presence_notes: Polite but almost entirely policy-recitation — the same scope denial is restated four times in near-identical language while clear emotional cues ('I can't believe it', 'you all shouldn't really do warehouse pick-ups') go completely unacknowledged, with no apology, empathy marker, or use of her name anywhere in the call.

The customer's clipped 'Okay. Okay. Okay.' runs and her sharp 'Really. Fu. Okay.' suggest real irritation, and since this was a service-recovery moment on a customer who has spent money twice this week, audio would confirm whether this needs a branch follow-up rather than just a coaching note.
